1 2. Heard the parties.

3. Having regard to the averments made in the instant application and submission made on behalf of the appellant, we are of the view that the appellant was prevented from sufficient cause in filing the appeal within Page 1 the period of limitation,as such, the delay of 89 days in preferring the instant appeal is hereby condoned.
4. Accordingly, the I.A. No. 3418 of 2023 stands allowed.

5. The appeal is under clause 10 of the Letter Patent is directed against the order dated 11.01.2023 passed by learned Single Judge of this Court in W.P.(C) No. 3569 of 2010 whereby and whereunder,
while dismissingthe writ petition the learned Single Judge has refused to pass positive direction with respect to the consideration of appointment which has been sought for by the petitioner in lieu of acquisition of land.

Factual Matrix 6. The brief facts of this case as per the pleadings made in the writ petition which read as under: -
7. The 2.48acres of land belonged to the father of the appellant /writ petitioner as it was acquired by the State for the purpose of mining activities by BCCL in L.A. Case No. 16 of 1984-85 and an award for compensation has been also passed pertaining to the aforesaid land, payment was also received by the father of the appellant after executing the required bond dated 07.09.1999.
8.

The father of the appellant/writ petitioner during his lifetime submitted representation for grant of service under Land Losers Scheme as back as on 27.07.1999, but no action was taken and thereafter, the appellant/writ petitioner filed several representations including representation dated 22.03.2007, but no action was taken.
Page 2 9.

Being aggrieved by non-consideration of the representation submitted by the appellant/writ petitioner for appointment under Land Losers Scheme, the appellant/writ petitioner moved a writ application before this Hon'ble Court being W.P.(C) 3569 of 2010.

10. The said writ petition was dismissed by the learned Single Judge vide order dated 11.01.2023 on the ground that much time has been elapsed from the date of acquisition and appellant/writ petitioner was minor on the date of acquisition.
It has also been observed by the learned Single Judge that respondents were not duty bound to give an employment as the compensation has already been accepted by the appellant's deceased father.
11. Hence, the present intra-court appeal.

2 12.
It is evident from the factual aspect that the land in question has been acquired way back in the year 1984-85 by the BCCL for mining activities.
13. The land acquisition proceeding has been proceeded, as an award for compensation, in favour of the father of the appellant/writ petitioner, has been passed.
14. The grievance of the appellant/ writ petitioner is that, as per the scheme, wherein the provision has been made to provide appointments in lieu of acquisition of land.

15. The compensation amount has been paid, so far as the land acquisition proceeding is concerned,
but no consideration has been given regarding the issue of appointment on compensate ground, not even during the lifetime of the father of the appellant/writ petitioner,who died in between the year 2002.
Page 3 16.

The appellant/writ petitioner thereafter attaining the majority has raised the grievance to provide appointment on compensate ground and representation to the respondents have been made by the appellant/writ petitioner dated 22.03.2007.
17.
The authority has declined to pass positive direction, being aggrieved, the writ petition has been filed being W.P.(C) No. 3569 of 2010.

18. The learned Single Judge, taking into consideration the fact that the day when the land was acquired or even the day when the father of the appellant had died, writ petitioner was minor and further the claim having been raised by the appellant/writ petitioner, after delay of 23 years, has declined to pass positive direction, against which the present letters patent appeal has been preferred.
Argument on behalf of the learned counsel for the appellant:
19.

Mr. Rajesh Kumar, learned counsel appearing for the appellant has submitted that the ground which has been taken to reject the claim of the appellant/writ petitioner cannot be said to be justified reason being that the delay of 23 years as has been levelled against the appellant/writ petitioner is not attributable to him rather, it is the respondents who have committed the delay, and as such, for the wrong committed by the respondents, appellant/ writ petitioner cannot be left to suffer.

20. It is submitted that the ground has also been taken that the land admittedly has been acquired andan award was prepared, as such, as per the scheme, the appointment was to be made in favour of the appellant/writ petitioner, Page 4 as the same has not been considered and when it was brought to the notice by filing the writ petition, even the learned Single Judge has not appreciated the aforesaid fact, therefore, the present intra court appeal has been preferred.

Argument on behalf of the learned counsel for the Respondent: -
21.

Mr. Anup Kumar Mehta, learned counsel appearing for the respondents has submitted by defending the impugned order that there is no error in the impugned order, since, the learned Single Judge has taken into consideration the fact that such claim has been made after lapse of 23 years from the date of the acquisition and the learned Single Judge on the basis of the same, considered such claim to be a belated claim.

22. The further ground has been taken that the day when the land was acquired the appellant/writ petitionerhad not attained the age of majority and there is a claim to provide appointment on compensate ground, only when he had attained the age of majority.
23. The learned counsel for the respondent based upon the aforesaid groundhas submitted that the order passed by the learned Single Judge cannot be said to be suffer from an error.
Analysis:-
24. We have heard the learned counsel for the parties and gone across the finding recorded by the learned Single Judge in the impugned order.
Page 5 25.
The undisputed fact in this case is that the land in question had been acquired sometime in the year 1984-85, then the proceeding had been initiated and accordingly, award was also passed.
26. The claim of the appellant/writ petitioner as per the scheme is forconsideration for appointment on compensate ground to the displaced persons.
27. The land was acquired while the father of the appellant/ writ petitioner was alive i.e., in the year 1984-85.

28. Further, it is not in dispute from the side of the petitioner that on the date of acquisition of land,
the petitioner was a minor.
Thus, it is evident that on the date of acquisition of land, the petitioner could not have been offered any employment.

29. The father of the appellant died in between the year 2002 and at that time as has been submitted on behalf of the learned counsel for the appellant/writ petitioner that the appellant/writ petitioner was minor at the time of acquisition.
He has raised the claim after attaining the majority.

30. Thus, it is admitted fact that at the time of acquisition of land, the writ petitioner-appellant was minor, which fact is obvious from the conduct of the appellant/writ petitioner that even though the land was acquired in the year 1984-85 but no such claim for employment has been made at that point of time but it is claimed by the appellant/writ petitioner that representation has been made in the year 2007 but it is settled position of law that filing of representation will not be a sufficient Bikash Singh Choudhary vs Bharat Coking Coal Ltd.

Page 6 31.

Reference in this regard be made to the judgment rendered by Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of State of Orissa Vs. Pyarimohan Samantaray & Ors reported in (1977) 3 SCC 396, wherein it has been laid down that making of repeated representation is not a satisfactory explanation of delay.

sentences.text:
For ready reference the aforesaid paragraph is being quoted as under:-
6.There is no satisfactory explanation of the inordinate delay for, as has been held by this Court in Rabindra Nath Bose v. Union of India [(1970) 1 SCC 84 : (1970) 2 SCR 697]

sentences.text: the making of repeated representations, after the rejection of one representation, could not be held to be a satisfactory explanation of the delay.
The fact therefore remains that the petitioner allowed some 11 years to go by before making a petition for the redress of his grievances.

In the meantime a number of other appointments were also made to the Indian Administrative Service by promotion from the State Civil Service, some of the officers received promotions to higher posts in that service and may even have retired.

Those who continued to serve could justifiably think that as there was no challenge to their appointments within the period prescribed for a suit, they could look forward to further promotion and higher terminal benefits on retirement.

The High Court therefore erred in rejecting the argument that the writ petition should be dismissed because of the inordinate and unexplained delay even though it was "strenuously" urged for its consideration on behalf of the Government of India.

32. Further in the case of Shiv Dass v. Union of India &Ors reported in (2007) 9 SCC 274, in particular paragraph 9, the Hon'ble Apex Court has observed that there is a limit to the time which can be considered reasonable for making representations and if the Government had turned down one representation the making of another representation on similar lines will not explain the delay.

9.It has been pointed out by this Court in a number of cases that representations would not be adequate explanation to take care of Page 7 delay.
This was first stated in K.V. Rajalakshmiah Setty v. State of Mysore [AIR 1967 SC 993].

33. The Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of State of Uttaranchal & Anr. Vs. Sri Shiv Charan Singh Bhandari & Ors. reported in2013 (6) SLR 629, while considering the issue regarding delay and laches has opined that repeated representations made will not keep the issues alive.

34.

It needs to refer herein that there is no period of limitation provided for filing a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution of India, but it is settled position of law that ordinarily, writ petition should be filed within a reasonable time 35.

In State of M.P. &Ors Vs. Nandlal Jaiswal & Ors reported in (1986) 4 SCC 566 , the Hon'ble Apex Court has observed that the power of the High Court to issue an appropriate writ under Article 226 of the Constitution is discretionary and if there is inordinate delay on the part of the petitioner in filing the writ petitioner and such delay is not satisfactorily explained, the High Court may decline to interfere and grant relief in exercise of its writ jurisdiction.

entities.text: State of M.P. &Ors Vs. Nandlal Jaiswal & Ors reported in (1986) 4 SCC 566
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Emphasis was laid down on the principle of delay and laches stating that the High Court does not ordinarily Page 8 permit a belated resort to the extraordinary remedy under the writ jurisdiction because it is likely to cause confusion and inconvenience in bringing the justice.

36. For ready reference the relevant paragraph of the aforesaid judgment is being quoted as under:
24.

Now, it is well settled that the power of the High Court to issue an appropriate writ under Article 226 of the Constitution is discretionary and the High Court in the exercise of its discretion does not ordinarily assist the tardy and the indolent or the acquiescent and the lethargic.

If there is inordinate delay on the part of the petitioner in filing a writ petition and such delay is not satisfactorily explained, the High Court may decline to intervene and grant relief in the exercise of its writ jurisdiction.
The evolution of this rule of laches or delay is premised upon a number of factors.

The High Court does not ordinarily permit a belated resort to the extraordinary remedy under the writ jurisdiction because it is likely to cause confusion and public inconvenience and bring in its train new injustices.

The rights of third parties may intervene and if the writ jurisdiction is exercised on a writ petition filed after unreasonable delay, it may have the effect of inflicting not only hardship and inconvenience but also injustice on third parties.

When the writ jurisdiction of the High Court is invoked, unexplained delay coupled with the creation of third party rights in the meanwhile is an important factor which always weighs with the High Court in deciding whether or not to exercise such jurisdiction.

We do not think it necessary to burden this judgment with reference to various decisions of this Court where it has been emphasised time and again that where there is inordinate and unexplained delay and third party rights are created in the intervening period, the High Court would decline to interfere, even if the State action complained of is unconstitutional or illegal.

We may only mention in the passing two decisions of this Court one in Ramana Dayaram Shetty v. International Airport Authority of India [(1979) 3 SCC 489 : AIR 1979 SC 1628 : (1979) 3 SCR Page 9 1014] and the other in Ashok Kumar Mishra v. Collector [(1980) 1 SCC 180 : AIR 1980 SC 112 : (1980) 1 SCR 491] .

6 been filed by the petitioner more than five months after the acceptance of the tender of the fourth respondent and during that period, the fourth respondent had incurred considerable expenditure, aggregating to about Rs 1.25 lakhs, in making arrangements for putting up the restaurant and the snack bar.

Of course, this rule of laches or delay is not a rigid rule which can be cast in a strait jacket formula, for there may be cases where despite delay and creation of third party rights the High Court may still in the exercise of its discretion interfere and grant relief to the petitioner.

But, such cases where the demand of justice is so compelling that the High Court would be inclined to interfere in spite of delay or creation of third party rights would by their very nature be few and far between.
Ultimately it would be a matter within the discretion of the court; ex hypothesi every discretion must be exercised fairly and justly so as to promote justice and not to defeat it.

37. Further, reference in this regard be made to the case of New Delhi Municipal Council Vs. Pan Singh &Ors reported in (2007) 9 SCC 278 in particular paragraph 17, which is quoted hereunder as:
17.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Although, there is no period of limitation provided for filing a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution of India, ordinarily, writ petition should be filed within a reasonable time.
(See Lipton India Ltd. v. Union of India).

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: 38. Thus, it is evident from the aforesaid settled proposition of law that the doctrine of delay and laches should not be lightly brushed aside.
A writ court is required to weigh the explanation offered and the acceptability of the same.
The Page 10 Court should bear in mind that it is exercising an extraordinary and equitable jurisdiction.
Conclusion 39.

Further, this Court is conscious with the fact that being a constitutional Court, it has a duty to protect the rights of the citizens but simultaneously it is to keep itself alive to the primary principle that when an aggrieved person, without adequate reason, approaches the Court at his own leisure or pleasure, the Court would be under legal obligation to scrutinize whether the lis at a belated stage should be entertained or not.
Be it noted, delay comes in the way of equity.

40. In certain circumstances delay and laches may not be fatal but, in most circumstances,
inordinate delay would only invite disaster for the litigant who knocks at the doors of the Court.

Delay reflects inactivity and inaction on the part of a litigant - a litigant who has forgotten the basic norms, namely, "procrastination is the greatest thief of time" and second, law does not permit one to sleep and rise like a phoenix.
Delay does bring in hazard and causes injury to the lis.
41. The law is well-settled that if no claim has been raised fairly within the reasonable period, then such litigation is not to be reopened on the principle of applicability of delay and latches.

42. Now coming to the facts of the instant case is wherein it is admitted that appellant/writ petitioner was minor, the day when the land was acquired and subsequently, he attained majority and thereby, the appellant/writ petitioner raised Page 11 the claim of compensate appointment after lapse of 23 years.

44. Accordingly, the instant Letters Patent Appeal stands dismissed.
